metadata.title: Vomiting and abdominal pain in a 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes
metadata.author: seed

patient.name: Sara Ahmed
patient.personality: Anxious, unwell, finds it hard to concentrate
patient.communication_style: Short answers, occasionally confused, breathing deeply

history.chief_complaint: Vomiting and tummy pain for a day, feeling very unwell

history_of_presenting_illness.onset: Symptoms began about 24 hours ago and have worsened
history_of_presenting_illness.vomiting: Several episodes, unable to keep fluids down
history_of_presenting_illness.thirst_and_urine: Very thirsty, passing large amounts of urine for 3 days
history_of_presenting_illness.breathing: Feels short of breath and is breathing heavily
history_of_presenting_illness.precipitant: Had a sore throat and fever last week; missed several insulin doses because she felt too nauseated to eat
history_of_presenting_illness.associated: Drowsy, tired, mild blurring of vision

drug_history: Basal-bolus insulin (admits poor adherence this week)

review_of_systems.genitourinary: No dysuria, no frequency beyond the polyuria
review_of_systems.gynaecological: Last menstrual period 2 weeks ago, not sexually active

general.appearance: Drowsy, dehydrated, acetone smell on breath

abdomen.examination: Generalised mild tenderness, no guarding, no rebound, bowel sounds present

neurology.examination: Drowsy but rousable, no focal deficit

extremities.examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor

laboratory.name: Urea & Electrolytes
laboratory.clinical_significance: Total body potassium is depleted despite the serum value; guides replacement

laboratory.name: Complete Blood Count
laboratory.clinical_significance: Common in DKA; may reflect the precipitating infection

laboratory.name: Urinalysis
laboratory.clinical_significance: Supports DKA; no clear urinary source of infection

laboratory.name: Serum Amylase
laboratory.clinical_significance: Abdominal pain is due to DKA, not pancreatitis

laboratory.name: Thyroid Function Tests
laboratory.clinical_significance: Not contributory to the acute presentation

bedside.name: ECG
bedside.result: Sinus tachycardia, no peaked T waves
bedside.clinical_significance: Baseline; monitors for hyperkalaemic changes during treatment

diagnosis.explanation: Known type 1 diabetic with insulin omission and an intercurrent infection presenting with hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis — the diagnostic triad of DKA. Kussmaul breathing, dehydration and abdominal pain are classic features.

emergency_management: ABCDE assessment and large-bore IV access
IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride
Potassium replacement once K is known and urine output confirmed
Hourly glucose and ketone monitoring; continuous cardiac monitoring
definitive_management: Continue insulin until ketones < 0.6 and acidosis resolved, then convert to subcutaneous insulin with overlap
patient_education: Never omit insulin even when not eating

items.description: Asked about a precipitating infection / illness
Considered pregnancy as a precipitant in a woman of childbearing age
Explained the situation and plan to the patient clearly
detection_cues: what we are going to do

pearls: DKA is defined by the triad: hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia/ketonuria and metabolic acidosis.
Serum potassium is often normal or high at presentation despite a large total-body deficit; it falls quickly once insulin starts.
Abdominal pain in DKA usually resolves with treatment of the acidosis.
pitfalls: Giving insulin before checking potassium and starting fluids.
Missing the precipitant (infection, insulin omission, pregnancy).
Anchoring on a surgical abdomen and delaying DKA treatment.
references: JBDS Guidelines for the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in adults
learning_objectives: Recognise the clinical and biochemical features of DKA.
Prioritise fluids, fixed-rate insulin and potassium management.
